paper_title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: ing us to revisit fundamental question: Memory has become an important component of long-horizon LLM agents, supporting recall across interaction histories and reuse of prior experience (Wang et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Gur et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a). Recent work has introduced increasingly diverse memory representations and management mechanisms (Chhikara et al., 2025a; Kang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026a), aiming to make relevant information easier to preserve and utilize, but often incur additional computation over the original context. As memory systems grow more complex, it remains unclear how much these operations improve over straightforward alternative, such as directly retrieve from the raw history. Surveying prior works, it shows many memory designs primarily compare against other memories, while naive RAG is often overlooked, and when included, its setup is also not always fully specified (Appendix B.2). Without retrieval baseline, the value of building memory remains entangled with the value of direct evidence retrieval, leaving its marginal or net value underexamined. So this suggests gap between the growing complexity of memory design and our understanding of whether and where that complexity actually helps, motivatWhat is the net value of memory over straightforward baseline like naive RAG? To study this question, we start from common setting, personal-agent conversational memory. We evaluate representative memory designs across several benchmarks and model backbones, using naive RAG as reference to assess the net value of memory. The results show that naive RAG remains strong baseline and many memory systems underperform it across diverse settings, indicating negative net value in these cases. But closer query-level comparison shows memory is not uniformly worse. It does solve some queries RAG misses, where organization or restructuring may help, while losing others that RAG already solves. We refer to the former as memory benefit and the latter as memory tax. When the tax outweighs the benefit, memory falls below RAG overall. These gains and losses suggest different view of memory. Memory goes far beyond purely beneficial augmentation as often treated in prior works, and can be better understood as doubleedged process that changes how information from raw history is structured and accessed. We view such changes as inevitable deviations from the raw history. These deviations give memory its dual nature. They are originally designed and intended to better serve the task, e.g., by organizing scattered facts, distilling preferences, etc., yet some may also have unintended harmful effects due to particular design choices, such as losing or obscuring evidence. Memory benefit and tax thus capture the two sides, and their balance defines the net value of memory, reflected in the external performance. Memory benefit reflects the intended gains of memory design, such as reorganization or abstraction, which is expected. So we focus more on how the memory tax emerges. We first examine faithfulness for how well the information survives memory process, and then accessibility for how easily the preserved information can be recalled or accessed. We further study robustness for reliability of memory across backbone changes. These dimensions characterize memory tax from system side, and its balance with memory benefit also highly depends on the task setting. Across more personalagent memory benchmarks, we find naive RAG already achieves high absolute scores, suggesting retrieval-friendly task setting with limited benchmark headroom for memory to deliver more benefit and thus making the tax more visible. Moreover, the benefit-tax view is generalizable and not tied to particular memory forms, as nontrivial memory operations can introduce both beneficial and harmful deviations from the source. We further examine this in experiential memory and world-model memory. Finally, we derive some design implications from the perspective of memory deviations and benefit-tax trade-offs. We focus on simple changes that can be applied to existing memories without introducing new architectures. We hope that the notion of memory tax can shift more attention from standalone memory performance to the net value of memory and its dissection into benefit and tax, thus informing more reliable memory design and evaluation. Our contributions are as follows:

sections.title: 2 Preliminary
sections.content: Long-term memory for agents maintains information from past interactions and selectively exposes it to the model at query time. Let the interaction history be = {h1, . . . , hT }, where each ht may contain user/agent messages, observations, or other types of content. memory system processes this history into persistent memory = I(H), where denotes the memory ingestion process. Given task query q, it retrieves relevant memory units = R(q, M) and generates an answer ˆy = G(q, C). Different systems instantiate as summaries, extracted facts, structured records, episodic entries, or other representations. Naive chunk-based RAG provides natural reference under this formulation. It keeps raw history with minimal processing and retrieves relevant chunks directly. We use it throughout this work as the comparison reference for assessing the net value of memory, and measured memory benefit and memory tax are thus relative to this reference.

sections.title: 4.2 Memory Tax - Faithfulness: How Well Is
sections.content: the Information Preserved? To trace where memory tax comes from, the first place to look is how well the memory system preserves past information. Memory operations like restructuring and compression may discard or distort evidence before retrieval begins, and such loss can not be recovered later, so we first investigate the faithfulness for memory system, at both the 4 Figure 3: Original performances vs. w/ gold memory units (bars), and the memory tax (quantified in scores) before and after having gold memory units (boxed numbers). macro level and micro level. For each query, we denote the raw conversation turns or steps with the evidence as gold raw turns, and the corresponding constructed memory units as gold memory units (null if the evidence is lost after construction). At the macro level, we replay QA with only the gold raw turns and, separately, only the gold memory units. Gold memory units remove retrieval failures, so the remaining memory tax reflects the losses introduced in memory construction, as shown by the red boxes in Figure 3. At the micro level, we sample some atomic facts from the raw corpus and trace each fact to its corresponding memory units, annotating the degree of information loss, as shown in Table 2 and information loss does exist in many systems. Appendix C.2 and D.2 have more details and case studies. Information loss with varying severity during the memory process becomes direct cause of memory tax. However, the reduced tax after having oracle memory also indicates degradation arises beyond construction. The performance shows similar signal. Some systems (MAGMA, LIGHTMEM) achieve gold-mem scores close to gold-raw-turn scores, yet far above their original, suggesting the preserved evidence may become harder to access.

sections.content: Can Stored Information Be Accessed? 4.2 examines how much information survives memory construction. However, preserved information is useful only if it remains accessible at query time. So next we measure the accessibility of memory from both macro and micro levels. At the macro level, we replay retrieval iteratively for multiple rounds over the constructed memory and record how many rounds are needed to recover all gold memory units for given query. Evidence lost in construction is marked as not retrievable. As shown in Figure 4, Memory systems Figure 4: Retrieval rounds replayed for the evidence to be fully retrieved, under raw chunks vs. memory units. Figure 5: Similarity comparison of (query, gold raw turn) vs. (query, gold memory unit), with overall distribution shift (left) and point-wise similarity difference (right). recover fewer queries than RAG in the first round, suggesting that some relevant evidence is buried deeper after memory construction. To understand why preserved evidence becomes harder to access, we further inspect some cases as the micro level analysis (Appendix D.3). We observe several recurring patterns where evidence is fragmented across multiple memory units, diluted with unrelated information, or rephrased, weakening its accessibility compared with raw history. To visualize this effect more broadly, we compare the (query, gold raw turn) similarity with the (query, gold memory unit) similarity, reporting the pointwise changes and overall drift in Figure 5. Since each system retrieves within its own memory store, absolute similarity values across systems are only indicative, the main signal is how memory construction shifts the query alignment of the same evidence. Appendix C.3 provides more results. Memory process can reduce evidence accessibility by fragmenting, diluting, or rephrasing it, creating memory tax even evidence is not lost.

sections.title: 4.5 Benchmark Headroom Further Exposes
sections.content: the Memory Tax The analysis so far focuses on how memory tax arises within memory system. Yet the balance between memory benefit and tax also depends on the task settings. Some tasks naturally favor direct recall from raw history, while others may benefit more from abstraction or distillation. To examine this evaluation-side effect, we run several naive baselines across broader set of long-term memory benchmarks, including 1 No Memory, 2 IDFkeyword, lexical matching baseline based on the keyword rarity, 3 RAG-Emb, and 4 RAG-Hybrid. Details are in Appendix C.5. Figure 7 shows that simple retrieval baselines already performs quite well on some of the benchmarks, including some widely-used ones. For example, the extremely simplified IDF-keyword based method can even achieve more than 50% in absolute score on some of them, while RAGHybrid reaches about 70%. Such results suggest some current evaluation settings are relatively retrieval-friendly, leaving quite limited headroom for heavy memory to improve over naive retrieval.

This also helps explain why some systems with lightweight or even no explicit memory construction can achieve strong performance and efficiency (Yan et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026b; Xiao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026b). When naive retrieval already provides strong baseline, they inherit much of that performance while introducing little memory tax, so lightweight design can be particularly competitive under limited benchmark headroom. On the other hand, many real-world queries are also naturally retrieval-friendly, making such accurate recall tasks essential and meaningful in its own right. Current benchmarks contain large share of such queries, and future evaluations could complement them with harder settings. Moreover, reporting memory systems alongside naive RAG can make remaining improvement room more explicit, which also helps clarify the contribution of built memory. RAG scores can also serve as reference for calibrating difficulty and leaving meaningful room for more reliable evaluations.

sections.title: 5 Generalizing Memory Tax
sections.content: Memory serves wide range of application scenarios beyond personal-agent memory. We next examine whether the same benefit-tax view extends to two substantially different settings.

sections.title: 6 Design Implications
sections.content: In this section, we derive some simple yet effective design implications for reducing or compensating for the memory tax. We focus on improvements that can be used on existing memory systems without introducing another new architecture, and deliberately exclude common test-time scaling techniques like retrieval depth / width expansion, query refinement, using stronger backbones, etc. 6.1 (Memory Construction) Make memory deviations more recoverable. As we discussed above, building memory can introduce changes and deviations from the raw history about how information is preserved and accessed through diverse memory operations. While no single design can predict and fit all tasks needs, 7 and the harmful deviations are difficult to eliminate entirely, more promising way to reduce memory tax is to make such deviations recoverable, preserving lightweight path back to the source history when memory becomes insufficient. As simple proof of concept, we retrieve from source history alongside normal memory retrieval and jointly rerank them before QA. This lightweight recovery path can restore evidence lost during construction or missed in access. Results in Table 4 show consistent improvements and reduction of memory tax across several memory systems. 6.2 (Memory Access) Recursive or selfreferential memory for retrieval. Memory tax can only be visible in actual use, when relevant evidences become harder to access and are recovered only after deep search. Such retrieval experience directly reflects the harmful deviations memory introduced, and can in turn provide feedback to improve future memory access, creating recursive loop between memory access and construction. Inspired by progress on recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Zhang et al., 2026c; Karten et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d), where system is expected to improve how it improves, memory can similarly remember how it remembers. Past queries, evidences, and retrieval paths can themselves be source materials for memory, and this is particularly useful for multi-round retrieval, since evidence found in deeper rounds can then be accessed directly by similar information needs. It also offers new dimension of test-time scaling at query-side, allowing inter-query scaling beyond single query. As simple proof of concept, we treat past queries and retrieved evidence as additional inputs into memory store, making them available for future retrieval. Results in Table 4 also validate its effectiveness. 6.3 (Future Direction and Beyond Memory Operations) Try modeling future demand beyond past information. Many methods build memory ahead of time (AoT) before future queries come. To cover broader range of possible queries, AoT systems may need to process more information in more elaborate ways, making it increasingly expensive. The opposite is just-in-time (JiT) memory (Yan et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026b; Yan et al., 2026a), which delays memory operations until queries arrive. With query already known, JiT can choose more targeted forms and directions of deviation to maximize the memory benefit and minimize the memory tax, but moves computation to the online part and increases user-facing latency, to which the users are highly sensitive. middle ground is to model the future demand. In personal agent settings, task queries are not purely random. Past interests, habits, and access patterns provide prior over what information is likely to matter, and hence what kinds of deviations that memory introduces are likely useful. Such signals may help construction allocate effort more selectively, and reduces harmful deviations, without paying the full online cost of JiT. From this view, memory can partly be seen as an implicit recommendation system that estimates future relevance of past information. Exploring this perspective in real-world personal-agent settings may be promising direction for future exploration.

sections.title: 7 Related Works
sections.content: Long-Term Agent Memory. Long-term memory has become an important component for longhorizon agents, supporting the retention of specific information, past interactions, and task experience. Existing systems explore variety of memory representations, including relatively flat stores (Liu et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026b; Meng et al., 2026), hierarchical organizations, from short- /long-term memory layers (Kang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026a) to filesystem-tree designs in recent industrial systems (Volcengine, 2026; Tencent-Cloud, 2026), and graph-based representations (Jiang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026a). Another line of variation lies in how memory operations are governed. Some systems rely on predefined harness for writing, updating, and using memories, while others allow an LLM agent to decide these operations dynamically (Wang and Chen, 2025; Xu et al., 2026a; EverMind-AI, 2026) or explore learned memory policies (Yan et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2026b). In this work, we study these memory systems through the lens of their net value, examining the gains and the losses introduced by memory operations. Empirical Studies of Agent Memory. Recent empirical studies examine agent memory from different perspectives, including how memory systems are designed and deployed, their performancecost trade-offs, and where computation and time are spent (Jiang et al., 2026b; Omri et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026; Wolff and Bennati, 2026). These works mainly characterize existing memory designs and their empirical behavior, but our work focuses on the net value introduced by memory processing itself. We introduce memory tax to characterize its losses relative to direct retrieval, analyze how such losses arise from both system and evaluation sides, and derive system-agnostic design implications.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We revisit the agent memory by studying its net value over direct retrieval from raw history. Across the evaluation on three benchmarks with many retrieval-friendly queries alongside some complex ones, many memory methods underperform naive RAG, indicating negative net value in these settings. We dissect this net value into memory benefit and tax, showing memory can improve how past information is organized and used, but may also have harmful effects. We analyze memory tax from both system sides and evaluation settings, and generalize it to broader scenarios like experiential memory and world-model memory. We hope memory tax can shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, and encourages more reliable memory design and evaluation.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Given the rapid development of this field, our baseline selection is representative rather than exhaustive. We also follow official configurations wherever possible, though further system-specific tuning may yield better performance. Our benchmarks are primarily static, offline, and Englishlanguage, leaving long-lived deployments with interleaved queries and multilingual interactions underexplored. Extending the analysis to other forms of memory, such as omnimodal, latent, and parametric memory, is also left for future work. Our evaluation is limited by computational and APIcalling cost. We do not include stronger frontier models beyond GPT-5.6 Luna (low), and use stratified subsets for some benchmarks (20% of PersonaMem-v2, 10% of MINT-Eval, and 20% LongMemEval-s questions for GPT-5.6 Luna).

sections.content: A.1 Benchmark Details Table 5 summarizes the evaluation data. LongMemEval-s (Wu et al., 2025). Each question has its own chat history of about 50 sessions, with few evidence sessions hidden among distractors. We use the full set, except 100-corpus subset stratified by question type for GPT-5.6 Luna. PersonaMem-v2 (Jiang et al., 2025b). Each corpus is one simulated users chat history (128k-token variant), with four-way MCQs on the users implicit persona and preferences. We evaluate 20% subset (40 of 200 corpora). sections.content: Retrieval scope. In existing comparisons of memory systems, the retrieval top-k used at QA time is usually inherited from each repositorys default configuration or aligned with that of the proposed system. Since memory units vary widely across systems, from single turn to merged chunk or session summary, the same top-k can span from few hundred to tens of thousands of tokens. So we measure Retrieval Scope (RS), defined as the fraction of tokens in memory units seen by the LLM from retrieval through QA over the total tokens in all memory units within the systems retrieval range. We average this ratio over questions and report it as percentage. Tokens are counted with the Qwen3.6-27B tokenizer. We adjust each systems top-k so that its RS is no lower than that of RAG (1-round), while keeping RS reasonably comparable across systems. We further clarify what counts as the docs LLM sees in RS. This depends on the LLMs involvement in retrieval, which falls into three levels: 1 no involvement, where retrieval relies entirely on embeddings, indices, or other non-LLM components. 2 pre-retrieval involvement, where LLM rewrites query or extracts keywords but reads no retrieved units. 3 retrieval-time involvement, where the LLM reads retrieved units, e.g., to decide whether further retrieval is needed, reformulate the query, or assess whether unit is useful. Only level 3 exposes the LLM to memory units beyond the final answer prompt. RS counts all such exposure, including every unit read from retrieval through QA regardless of whether it appears in the final answer context. Both the numerator and denominator count only content that participates in retrieval. Metadata attached to memory units, such as topic, involved people, or date, is excluded when it is not searched over. The RS requirement has some exceptions. Some memory systems produce only few memory units, each covering large part of the corpus. Forcing their RS to match would leave very small top-k, as for OpenViking, so we fix top-k for them. Inference settings. We use NVIDIA H20 GPUs to locally served Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.5-4B, and they are decoded with temperature 0.0 and top-p 1.0 for every ingestion and QA call, with reasoning disabled. GPT-5.6 Luna (low) is accessed through the OpenAI API with the default sampling config and reasoning effort set to low. For fair comparison, we unify the embedding model and, where system uses one, the reranker model across all baselines. Unless otherwise stated, all baselines use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b) as the embedding model and Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b) as the reranker if used in certain memory system. A.5 More Explanations GPT-5.6 luna on PersonaMem-v2. Interestingly, on PersonaMem-v2 5.6-luna usually scores lower than Q3.6-27B for most systems, while on LongMemEval-s and MINT-Eval, its usually better. Our inspection suggests this gap reflects answer preference of 5.6-luna, not the ability degradation. PersonaMem-v2 often contrasts personalized answer with an almost identical generic distractor, and 5.6-luna tends to prefer the generic option. This preference appears to interact with 5.6-lunas tendency to avoid relying on stereotypes, healthrelated, or privacy-sensitive information. This pattern is specific to PersonaMem-v2, whose multiplechoice questions often reward explicit use of user preferences, unlike the other two benchmarks. Gold Context baseline on MINT-Eval. MINTEval provides author-annotated gold context for only about half of its queris, so we skip it.

sections.content: We largely follow the official configurations of each memory baseline as closely as possible. When modifications are necessary for controlled comparison, we further examine their impact to ensure that they DO NOT artificially disadvantage the corresponding baseline. Shared settings. For fair comparison, we standardize several evaluation components across baselines, including the QA prompt, QA backbone, judge prompt, judge backbone, and embedding model. Baseline Details. 6 baselines adopted: I3DM (Li et al., 2026) retrieves the past frames most relevant to the current viewpoint with implicit 3D-aware matching and injects them as conditioning, so its memory is the naive past frames. FRAMEPACK (Zhang et al., 2026e) packs the 25 number of rounds for that store. We observe three recurring patterns: Fragmenting: one raw turn is split into several units, and unit carrying necessary part of the evidence ranks far behind the others. Diluting: the evidence is wrapped in unrelated or additional content, such as long profile or an elaborated note, which weakens its match with the query. Rephrasing: the evidence is rewritten, sometimes with slight shift in meaning, and no longer matches the query as well as the raw wording. D.4 Direct Examples for the Double-edged

sections.title: D Case Studies
sections.content: In this section, we show some representative case studies for both Memory Benefit (D.1) and Memory Tax ( D.2 , D.3 ), and also some comparison examples of benefit and tax within the same memory mechanism to directly show the dual nature of memory (D.4). D.1 Memory Benefit Even the main results show memory underperform RAG in the overall performance in many cases, memory systems can still answer some questions correctly where naive RAG fails and we still need them in such scenarios. We inspect sample of such questions and group the wins of memory into several representative types (Figures 18 and 19): Focused atomic extraction: each fact becomes short unit, so the gold facts fit into the retrieved context, while RAGs top-k is filled by long chunks that other irrelevant information, making the evidence hard to recover. Multi-hop linking: facts from different sessions are retrieved together and combined, while for naive RAG the evidences are scattered. Implicit preference exposure: trait mentioned only in passing becomes an explicit unit in the memory. Temporal anchoring: relative time expressions are anchored to absolute dates during construction. Explicit forgetting: forget request updates the stored state by removing or deactivating the targeted content. Processing for heterogeneous inputs: nondialogue inputs such as code diffs are described in natural language, making it easier to be recalled with semantic retrieval. sections.title: F Prompt Templates
sections.content: F.1 QA Prompts QA Prompt: General QA [SYSTEM] You are helpful assistant with long-term memory of your past conversations with the user. Answer the users question based on your memories. Follow these rules: 1. Be concise and specific. For dates use the format "15 July 2023"; for durations answer in years/months/days. 2. Time: reason from the timestamps attached to your memories and from the current date given with the question. Resolve relative expressions ("last year", "how long ago") against the current date, not against when the conversation happened. 3. Conflicts: if memories disagree because something changed over time, trust the most recent memory, unless the question asks about an earlier point in time. 4. The needed evidence may be scattered across several conversations; combine related memories before answering. 5. Do not make up information. If the needed information does not appear in your memories, say that the information is not available. [USER] <MEMORY> [[MEMORY BLOCK]] (OPTIONAL USER PROFILE SECTION:) <USER PROFILE> [[USER PROFILE]] Current date: [[QUESTION DATE]] Question: [[QUESTION]] Answer concisely, providing only the answer content. Table 22: QA prompt for general (open-ended) questions. The user-profile section is omitted when no profile is available for this memory system. QA Prompt: Open-ended Preference QA [SYSTEM] You are helpful assistant with long-term memory of your past conversations with the user. Answer the users question based on your memories. Follow these rules: 1. Be concise and specific. For dates use the format "15 July 2023"; for durations answer in years/months/days. 2. Time: reason from the timestamps attached to your memories and from the current date given with the question. Resolve relative expressions ("last year", "how long ago") against the current date, not against when the conversation happened. 3. Conflicts: if memories disagree because something changed over time, trust the most recent memory, unless the question asks about an earlier point in time. 4. The needed evidence may be scattered across several conversations; combine related memories before answering. [USER] <MEMORY> [[MEMORY BLOCK]] (OPTIONAL USER PROFILE SECTION:) <USER PROFILE> [[USER PROFILE]] Current date: [[QUESTION DATE]] Question: [[QUESTION]] Read all sentences carefully and extract the information that may be relevant to the question step by step. Your answer should fully consider the users preferences. Table 23: QA prompt for fully open-ended preference questions (e.g., the single-session-preference questions of LongMemEval), which have no single reference answer. Compared with Table 22, the rule on unavailable information is dropped and the answer is asked to take the users preferences into account. The following are relevant excerpts from your conversation history with this user. Use them to personalize your response. [USER] <MEMORY> [[MEMORY BLOCK]] (OPTIONAL USER PROFILE SECTION:) <USER PROFILE> [[USER PROFILE]] <QUESTION> [[QUESTION]] QA Prompt: MCQ (continued) <CANDIDATE RESPONSES> A. [[CANDIDATE A]] B. [[CANDIDATE B]] C. [[CANDIDATE C]] D. [[CANDIDATE D]] Which candidate response best fits this user? Answer with one letter (A, B, or D) and nothing else. No explanation. F.2 LLM-as-Judge Prompts LLM-as-Judge Prompt: Short QA (General) will give you question, correct answer, and response from model. Please check whether the response is correct or not. If the meaning of response is equivalent to the correct answer or the response contains all the intermediate steps to get the correct answer, you should also answer CORRECT. Notes: - For time related questions, both the gold answer and the generated answer can be specific date, month, year, or relative time reference (like "last Tuesday" or "next month"). Try your best to convert relative time reference to specific date/time and compare them in the same format - as long as the generated answer refers to the same date or time period as the gold answer, it should be counted as CORRECT. - For rounding issues, such as the reference answer being 2 months and the generated answer being 2 months and 3 days; These cases should be counted as CORRECT. Question: [[QUESTION]] Gold answer: [[GOLD ANSWER]] Model Response: [[GENERATED ANSWER]] Just return the label CORRECT or WRONG in json format with the key as "label". Table 25: General LLM-as-Judge prompt for short-answer questions. LLM-as-Judge Prompt: Open-ended Question will give you question, rubric for desired personalized response, and response from model. Please output CORRECT if the response satisfies the desired response. Otherwise, output WRONG. The model does not need to reflect all the points in the rubric. The response is correct as long as it recalls and utilizes users personal information correctly. Question: [[QUESTION]] Rubric: [[GOLD ANSWER]] Model Response: [[GENERATED ANSWER]] You may provide reasoning, but you MUST end your response with your final answer following the format: Just return the label CORRECT or WRONG in json format with the key as "label". Table 26: LLM-as-Judge prompt for LongMemEval single-session-preference questions. LLM-as-Judge Prompt: MCQ will give you 4-way multiple-choice question, its options, the correct option, and response from model whose reply could not be parsed into clean option letter. Your job is to decide which option the models response actually commits to, and whether that is the correct one. Notes: - The model often quotes or paraphrases an options text instead of giving its letter. Match on meaning, not on exact wording. - Output CORRECT only if the response commits to exactly one option AND that option is the correct one. - Output WRONG if the response is empty, refuses to answer, hedges between several options, restates the question, or commits to an option that is not the correct one. - Do not reward response for merely sounding sensible or helpful. It must select the correct option. Question: [[QUESTION]] Options: [[OPTIONS BLOCK]] Correct option: [[GOLD LETTER]]. [[GOLD ANSWER]] Model Response: [[GENERATED ANSWER]] Just return the label CORRECT or WRONG in json format with the key as "label".
